points.heading: Deepen: two-word times
points.body:
Today only the **two-word** path: **helper** haber + participle (-ado/-ido), the **already-done** form. ## Key idea Let's explore together. Listen to the same participle with different helpers: he cantado, había cantado, habré cantado, habría cantado. The participle stays; the **helper** moves. ## More examples One-word clock: **canto / cantaba / canté / cantaré / cantaría**. Two-word clock: **he cantado / había comido / habré vivido / habría terminado**. Choose: «Yesterday I **finished**» (one closed word) vs «I **have finished** already» (two words). Story mix: «I **was reading** when the phone **rang**.» Practice: Now it's your turn. With participle comido, write he / habías / habremos / habría + comido. Mark helper and participle, then invent one real-life sentence with he comido.

Práctica: Ahora te toca a ti.

lesson.summary: This lesson teaches practice two-word times. Understand the central idea first, then explore it, practice it, and check a common mistake.
lesson.memoryPhrase: One word: **canto / cantaba / canté / cantaré / cantaría**. Two words: helper **haber** + already-done form (**he cantado**).
lesson.weekRecap: One word: canto / cantaba / canté / cantaré / cantaría. Two words: helper haber + already-done form (he cantado). Learn to narrate WHEN an action happens: one-word forms and two-word forms (haber + already-done form), choosing with meaning.
lesson.priorDayRecap: Deepen: one-word times. Today we stay on the one-word path only (no haber). Keep the thread: verb = action; conjugate = change for who/when; stem = fixed part; ending = tip.

questions.prompt: Which Spanish form shows an action happening now?
Which form tells about a finished action yesterday?

choices: A repeated or ongoing past action.
questions.answer: A repeated or ongoing past action.

questions.prompt: What two parts make a compound tense?
choices: A form of haber and a participle.
questions.answer: A form of haber and a participle.

questions.prompt: In «he cantado», which word is the participle?
Why should «comido» stay the same in «hemos comido»?
choices: It is always a future word.
The participle does not become plural for the subject.
questions.answer: The participle does not become plural for the subject.
